# Skills for agents

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/docs/reference.ts. Do not edit; run `pnpm docs:reference`. -->

A skill is a short set of rules, with numbers, for one step of making a video: what to ask before building, timing in frames, where text may go at every aspect ratio, motion curves and durations, camera moves and cuts, how moving things and people behave so the result does not look fake, loudness and voice, caption limits, sync tolerances, brand consistency and the checks before delivery.
Each rule carries its number and its source (published standards such as EBU, ITU, WCAG and Netflix or BBC timed text; animation and cinematography practice; physics) and says which tools and fields apply it here. Where the studio enforces a number, a test keeps the skill and the check identical.
An agent that reads the skill for the step it is on makes fewer of the defaults that make a video look generic.

## Reading them

| Where | How |
| --- | --- |
| MCP | `get_skill` without `name` lists them; `get_skill { name }` returns one as Markdown. Resources `renderweld://skills` (the index) and `renderweld://skills/<name>`. |
| REST | `GET /v1/skills` (the list) and `GET /v1/skills/:name` (`text/markdown`). Both need the `read` scope. |
| Agent tools | `renderweld skills export <dir>` writes `<dir>/renderweld-<name>/SKILL.md` for each skill, the folder layout Claude Code (`.claude/skills/`), Codex and other agent tools load. `--prefix` changes the folder prefix; a changed file is kept unless `--force`. `renderweld skills list` prints them. |

The workflow guide (`renderweld://guide/workflow`, the `make_reel` prompt) starts with the brief and points to the skills.

## Adding your own

Set `skills.dir` (`RENDERWELD_SKILLS_DIR`) to a folder of skills: your house rules, or a skills pack. They are served beside the built-in ones, and one with a built-in's name replaces it.

- Each skill is `<name>.md` or `<name>/SKILL.md`, the Agent Skills format: front matter with `name` (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, matching the file or folder name) and `description` (at most 1024 characters; say when to use it), `title` optional, then Markdown.
- At most 256 KiB a skill and 200 skills.
- The folder is read at start-up. A file that cannot be used stops the start with its name, so a broken pack is never served half-loaded.

```markdown
---
name: house-style
description: Our lower thirds, logo placement and words we never use. Use for every video for the Acme brand.
---
# House style

1. The logo sits bottom right, 4 % of the short side, on every scene.
```

<a id="video-brief"></a>

## Video brief

`video-brief`: Turn a request into a written brief before building anything, so the manifest comes from the user's answers, not from guesses. Use when a new video starts, or when its goal, platform or length changes.

**Use when:** a new video starts, or the goal, platform or length changes.
A model fills every gap you leave with a default, and defaults are what make
videos look generic. Ask, or write the default down and mark it assumed.

### Rules
1. Never infer the goal, audience, platform or length from style words
   ("modern", "engaging"). Ask, or state the default and label it *assumed*.
2. Ask only what the request has not already answered, in one message: at
   most about eight questions (group related topics), each with a suggested
   default the user can accept with "yes". The topics:
   goal (one sentence: "after watching, <who> will <do what>"), audience and
   language, where it is posted (platform, organic or paid), size or sizes,
   length, tone (three adjectives, each turned into something measurable such
   as pace or colour), brand (logo, colours, fonts), the one call to action,
   captions (burned, sidecar file, both, which languages), voice (human or
   synthetic, accent, pace), music (licence source) and anything that must
   appear word for word.
3. Take sizes and limits from the platform's current spec, not from memory.
   Size is never assumed: if the user did not say, ask; there is no "usual"
   aspect ratio.
4. Every factual claim in the video traces to a source the user gave you;
   otherwise leave it out. Never invent numbers, quotes or testimonials.
5. Record the licence of every asset you add (music, fonts, footage, images,
   a voice or likeness). A cloned or synthetic voice of a real person needs
   that person's consent, from the user.
6. If the video shows realistic synthetic people or events, decide with the
   user how it will be disclosed on the platform it goes to.
7. List the deliverables: every size, language, caption file and cut-down.
8. Read the brief back as a short table and wait for an explicit yes before
   writing scenes. Keep open questions listed; do not resolve them yourself.

### In RenderWeld
- The `brief_intake` prompt asks the open questions in one message; use it.
- Store the answers in the manifest `brief`: `goal`, `audience`, `style`,
  `platform`, `targetSeconds`. `validate_project` warns when the total length
  is more than 10 % off `targetSeconds`.
- `brief.platform` changes the safe areas of tall frames (see
  `layout-and-type`). Extra sizes are `variants`; each may set its own
  `platform`.
- Asset licences go in `upload_asset` / `add_asset_from_url` (`license`);
  `validate_project` warns about assets without one.
- Captions: `update_captions { mode }`; voice: `generate_voice` needs the
  user's agreement to the cost (`acknowledgeCost: true`).

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- A silent default size and length nobody asked for.
- Tone words with no numbers behind them; invented statistics.
- Default "upbeat" music chosen without the user.

### Before you render
- [ ] Goal sentence, audience, platform, size(s), length and the call to action are the user's, or marked assumed and confirmed.
- [ ] Caption mode, voice and music decided with the user; every asset has a licence.
- [ ] Every claim has a source; disclosure decided where it applies.
- [ ] The user said yes to the brief.

### Sources
- OpenAI, Sora 2 prompting guide: unstated details are invented by the model (developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/sora/sora2_prompting_guide).
- US FTC, advertising substantiation policy (ftc.gov).
- YouTube and TikTok policies on labelling realistic synthetic content (support.google.com/youtube/answer/14328491; tiktok.com/transparency).

<a id="script-timing"></a>

## Script timing

`script-timing`: Fit words, reading and scenes into the time available, in frames. Use when writing or editing on-screen text, voice-over lines or scene durations. (What the video says, and its structure, is the user's decision.)

**Use when:** writing on-screen text or voice-over, or setting scene lengths.
This skill is arithmetic, not taste: what the video says and how it is
structured come from the brief and the user.

### Rules
1. Work in frames. frames = round(seconds × fps), converted once from
   absolute times; never add up rounded scene lengths and convert again.
2. Voice-over budget: words = seconds × words-per-minute ÷ 60. At 150 wpm
   that is 2.5 words a second (a 30 s video holds about 75 words; at an
   explainer's 130 wpm, 65: `voice-over` rule 1). Leave 10-15 % of the
   running time without narration.
3. On-screen text needs time to be read: at least 0.33 s per word, and at
   least characters ÷ 20 seconds, whichever is longer, counted from when the
   text has finished arriving, not from when it starts to animate. (Captions
   have their own limits: `captions-and-accessibility`.)
4. The first frame is never empty: platforms use it as a thumbnail and a
   scroll decision is made on it.
5. One idea per scene. If a scene needs two sentences of explanation, it is
   two scenes.
6. Do not leave more than about 3 s without a visible change (new text, a
   cut, a move), unless the stillness is the point.
7. The last line or card holds still for at least 2 s.
8. Write for the ear: active voice, one claim per sentence, sentences of 20
   words or fewer; numbers and abbreviations written as they are spoken.
9. Read the script aloud with a timer before rendering; the measured time,
   not the estimate, decides the scene lengths.

### In RenderWeld
- Scene length: `durationSeconds` (rounded to frames) or `durationFrames`;
  every edit returns `timing` with each scene's start frame and length.
- Template minimum and maximum durations come from `list_templates`; out of
  range is a validation error.
- A voice-over with word timestamps (`generate_voice`) gives exact speech
  times; set scene lengths from them instead of from estimates.
- `validate_project` warns about scenes under 0.25 s and about a total more
  than 10 % (at least 1 s) away from `brief.targetSeconds`.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Text that disappears before it can be read; a wall of words on one card.
- Narration that runs over the end, or describes exactly what is on screen.
- An empty or logo-only first frame.

### Before you render
- [ ] Words fit the budget at the chosen pace; the script was read aloud and timed.
- [ ] Every text line has its reading time after it has fully appeared.
- [ ] First frame shows the subject; final card holds 2 s.

### Sources
- BBC Subtitle Guidelines (reading rates; bbc.co.uk/accessibility/forproducts/guides/subtitles).
- Netflix Timed Text Style Guide (20 characters a second; partnerhelp.netflixstudios.com).
- Voice-over pacing of 140-160 wpm is common practitioner guidance; measure your own voice.

<a id="layout-and-type"></a>

## Layout and type

`layout-and-type`: Safe areas for every aspect ratio, type sizes relative to the frame, contrast, line length and lower thirds. Use whenever you place text, a logo or interface elements.

**Use when:** placing any text, logo or UI, at any size or aspect ratio.

### Rules
1. Keep text inside the title-safe area and important action inside
   action-safe. On 16:9, graphics-safe is 5 % from each edge and action-safe
   3.5 % (EBU R 95). Square and 4:5: keep text inside the central 90 % × 90 %.
2. Tall frames (9:16) on social platforms are covered by the app's own
   buttons, captions and account name. Use the platform's published overlay
   for the exact zones; when one video goes to several platforms, stay inside
   all of them. A conservative fallback for 1080×1920: about 14 % clear at
   the top, 35 % at the bottom and 6 % at each side.
3. Size type from the frame's height, not in fixed pixels: titles about
   4-9 % of the frame height, secondary text 3-4 %, and nothing smaller than
   2.6 % of the shorter side (which decides on landscape frames). Check a copy scaled to 360 px wide: if you
   cannot read it there, it is too small for a phone.
4. Titles: at most two lines and about 37 characters a line. Avoid
   paragraphs on screen.
5. Contrast: at least 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text (WCAG 2.2,
   1.4.3), measured against the busiest frame behind it. Over video or
   photos, put the text on a solid box or a dark scrim.
6. One focal point per frame; at most two type families and three sizes per
   scene; no uppercase text with wide letter-spacing as decoration.
7. Use a grid: margins equal to the safe area, and recurring elements
   (lower thirds, captions, logo) in the same place in every scene.
8. A lower third sits inside the safe area and stays for its reading time
   (`script-timing` rule 3) plus about 0.5 s. Captions move up while a lower third is on screen.
9. Wider than 16:9 (21:9): compose so the important part also works in a
   16:9 crop.
10. Re-lay out each size; never centre-crop one size into another.

### In RenderWeld
- `--rf-unit` is 1 % of the shorter side; size and space everything in it so
  scenes reflow for every output and variant.
- `--rf-safe-top/right/bottom/left` are the safe insets for this output and
  platform (`--rf-title-safe-*`, `--rf-action-safe-*` too); keep text inside
  them. `brief.platform` (or a variant's `platform`) is free text: `none`,
  `broadcast`, `web` or `presentation` turn the app-interface zone of tall
  frames off; any other value (`tiktok`, `reels`) keeps it on.
- Layout templates (`html-layout` and its twins on the other engines) give
  split screen, picture-in-picture, grids and a lower third that reflow for
  every size.
- Built-in templates fit text to their boxes; long text gets smaller, so
  keep it short instead of relying on the fit.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Text under the app's buttons or touching the frame edge.
- Gradient text, glows, stacked drop shadows, emoji used as icons.
- Five fonts; everything centred with no grid.

### Before you render
- [ ] Every size checked on a frame with the platform overlay in mind.
- [ ] Contrast measured on the worst frame; text readable at 360 px wide.
- [ ] Reading times met (see `script-timing`).

### Sources
- EBU R 95, safe areas for 16:9 production (tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r095.pdf); ITU-R BT.1848.
- W3C WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.4.3 (w3.org/TR/WCAG22).
- BBC Subtitle Guidelines (line lengths and regions).
- TikTok, YouTube and Meta safe-zone overlays (ads.tiktok.com; services.google.com/fh/files/misc/universalsafezones-youtube.pdf).

<a id="motion-design"></a>

## Motion design

`motion-design`: Easing, durations in frames, staggering, springs and holds, so animation reads as designed rather than default. Use when animating text, shapes, UI or whole scenes.

**Use when:** animating anything: text, shapes, UI, images or scene entrances.

### Rules
1. Apply the classic principles of animation: slow in and slow out, arcs,
   anticipation, follow-through and overlap, staging, and exaggeration used
   sparingly.
2. Never move things with linear timing, except rotation, progress bars or a
   deliberate constant speed.
3. Ease by role: entrances decelerate (cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1)); exits
   accelerate (cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)); moves within the frame use a
   standard curve (cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)); camera moves ease in and out.
4. Durations, at 30 fps: small UI changes 6-8 frames (200-270 ms); text and
   object entrances 9-18 frames (0.3-0.6 s); large moves up to 21 frames
   (0.7 s). Over 0.4 s feels slow for small elements.
5. Exits are 40-50 % shorter than entrances.
6. Stagger related items so the next starts while the previous one is
   still moving, never after it has finished: list items 40-80 ms apart
   (one to three frames at 30 fps), words 60-120 ms, letters one frame.
7. Springs: think in damping ratio. 1.0 never overshoots; 0.7-0.85 feels
   premium; 0.4-0.6 playful; below 0.3 cartoonish. Position and scale may
   overshoot; opacity and colour never do.
8. Anticipation: 2-4 frames of counter-movement before a big move.
   Follow-through: parts settle 2-6 frames after the main body stops.
9. When something has arrived, it holds dead still. No drifting, breathing
   or pulsing to fill time.
10. One focal motion at a time. If a scene feels busy, remove about a third
    of the motion.
11. Use a small set of motion tokens per brand (about three durations and
    three curves) and keep them across the video.
12. Vary entrances between scenes. Between scenes, cut (`camera-language`);
    a transition is the exception, from one family (`brand-consistency`
    rule 7) and motivated by something on screen.

### In RenderWeld
- html and hyperframes scenes: CSS animations and the Web Animations API are
  seeked frame by frame, so timing is exact; write durations as CSS times
  computed from frames (frames ÷ fps). `--rf-speed` is the theme's speed
  multiplier (`motionSpeed`); multiply durations by it if you honour it.
- Built-in templates have their own timing; change their pace with the
  theme's `motionSpeed`, not by stretching the scene.
- Look at the motion before the final render: `preview_scene` renders one
  scene at low resolution.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Every element fades in and slides up the same way.
- Elastic bounce on interface elements; typewriter effect on every line.
- Titles that keep floating after they land; everything starting at once.

### Before you render
- [ ] No linear tweens on position, scale or opacity.
- [ ] Exits shorter than entrances; landed elements hold still.
- [ ] A preview of the busiest scene checked frame by frame around its main move.

### Sources
- Thomas & Johnston, *The Illusion of Life* (1981): the twelve principles.
- Material Design motion: duration and easing (m1.material.io/motion/duration-easing.html).
- IBM Carbon motion guidelines and tokens (carbondesignsystem.com/elements/motion/overview).

<a id="camera-language"></a>

## Camera language

`camera-language`: Shot sizes, framing, camera moves with speed limits, parallax, motion blur and cutting rules. Use for virtual camera moves (pan, zoom, Ken Burns), for prompts to video generators, and when deciding where to cut.

**Use when:** moving a virtual camera, panning or zooming an image or clip,
writing a prompt for a video generator, or editing cuts.

### Rules
1. Name each shot: extreme wide, wide, medium, medium close-up, close-up,
   extreme close-up. Plan the sequence of sizes; avoid two near-identical
   framings in a row.
2. Between two shots of the same subject, change the angle by at least 30°
   or the shot size clearly; otherwise the cut looks like a jump.
3. Keep the camera on one side of the line of action, so movement and gaze
   keep the same screen direction.
4. Composition: rule of thirds or a deliberate centre; eyes on the upper
   third in close shots; leave room in the direction of gaze or movement.
5. One camera move per shot. Combining push, pan, tilt and zoom at once
   looks unstable, and video generators handle it poorly.
6. Pan speed: at 24 fps with a 180° shutter, an object should take at least
   about 7 seconds to cross the frame at the move's fastest point, or it
   judders; higher frame rates judder less. Whip pans are the deliberate
   exception.
7. Motion blur follows the 180° shutter: exposure is 1 ÷ (2 × fps), so
   1/48 s at 24 fps and 1/60 s at 30 fps. Synthetic blur is about half the
   distance moved in one frame.
8. Push-ins and pan-and-zoom on stills: ease in and out, with a reason for
   the start and end framing; scale change of 20 % or less per 5 s; never
   zoom past the image's native resolution.
9. Parallax: two or three layers, speed in proportion to depth, never on
   text.
10. Avoid motion that causes discomfort: constant rotation, large fast
    full-frame movement, shake on graphics. Non-essential motion is an
    accessibility concern (WCAG 2.3.3).
11. Cut on action, in the middle of a movement, with matching direction and
    speed; keep the next point of interest near the last one.
12. Hard cuts by default. A dissolve says time has passed; do not crossfade
    between unrelated scenes.

### In RenderWeld
- Scenes play back to back with hard cuts; motivated transitions inside a
  scene are your own HTML/CSS.
- A camera move on an image or clip in an html scene: animate `transform`
  (translate and scale) of the media element with an ease-in-out curve over
  the scene; keep the scale change within rule 8.
- When prompting a generative video provider, write one shot size, one angle
  and one move with its speed per clip.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- A slow push on every shot; drone-style orbits on everything.
- Random tilted angles; whip pans between every scene.
- Jump cuts between near-identical framings; zooming into static UI.

### Before you render
- [ ] A shot list with size, angle, move and speed for each shot.
- [ ] Screen direction consistent; pan speeds within the limit.
- [ ] Frames just before and after each cut checked.

### Sources
- Christopher J. Bowen, *Grammar of the Edit* and *Grammar of the Shot* (30-degree and 180-degree rules).
- RED, camera panning speed and shutter angle guides (red.com/red-101).
- Walter Murch, *In the Blink of an Eye* (cutting priorities).
- W3C WCAG 2.2, 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions.

<a id="physical-plausibility"></a>

## Physical plausibility

`physical-plausibility`: Gravity, arcs, inertia, contact, squash limits, human gait, blinking and lip sync in frames, plus the artefact sweep for generated footage. Use when animating objects, people or animals, when choosing or prompting generated clips, and in review.

**Use when:** anything falls, bounces, walks, talks or is pushed; when you use
generated footage; when reviewing.
Viewers judge weight and timing instantly. Motion that breaks physics reads
as fake even when every frame looks sharp.

### Rules
1. Falling: time = √(2 × height ÷ 9.81). From 0.5 m that is about 0.32 s
   (10 frames at 30 fps), from 1 m 0.45 s (14 frames), from 2 m 0.64 s
   (19 frames). The distance covered grows every frame: never fall at a
   constant speed.
2. Thrown objects follow a parabola: constant horizontal speed, slowest at
   the top. Each bounce is lower and shorter than the one before, then the
   object rests.
3. Bigger things move more slowly: timing grows roughly with the square root
   of size.
4. Inertia: heavy objects start and stop on long eases; light ones react
   quickly and overshoot more. A push has a reaction and a recoil.
5. Contact: nothing passes through anything; feet stay planted while they
   carry weight (no sliding); resting objects have a contact shadow.
6. Squash and stretch keeps volume. Rigid objects (phones, cars, logos)
   never squash; soft ones stay within about 20 % in a realistic style.
7. Hair, cloth and straps lag the body by a few frames, then settle.
8. Walking is about 100-120 steps a minute (a step about every 12 frames at
   24 fps); running 160-180. Arms swing opposite to the legs.
9. Eyes: about 10-20 blinks a minute, each 0.1-0.4 s (3-12 frames at
   30 fps), at uneven intervals; the eyes lead a head turn and always look
   at something.
10. Lip sync: lips close fully on M, B and P; mouth shapes lead the sound by
    one or two frames.
11. Animals: copy the order of their legs from reference footage (the
    Muybridge photographs are in the public domain).
12. One lighting logic per scene: shadows agree in direction and softness
    across shots.
13. Generated footage: keep clips short, with one action and one camera move;
    avoid hands handling objects, liquids, breaking glass and crowds; cut
    away before a failure. Current models still fail physical tests often
    while looking realistic.
14. Sweep every generated clip frame by frame: count fingers, check objects
    stay the same through occlusion, check faces, clothes and logos do not
    drift between shots, look for garbled text on signs, flicker, floating,
    sliding and morphing, and unnatural blinking or skin.

### In RenderWeld
- Compute fall and bounce timings in frames before writing CSS keyframes;
  give each segment its own curve (ease-in on the way down, ease-out on the
  way up), not one linear keyframe list.
- Use `preview_scene` and check the frames around the contact moment.
- Generated clips are assets: record their source and licence, and log the
  artefact sweep in your review notes.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Floaty, weightless motion; bounces that get higher.
- Skating feet; melting or extra fingers; wobbling logos.
- Shadows that disagree; people who never blink.

### Before you render
- [ ] Fall and arc timings computed, not guessed.
- [ ] Planted frames locked; rigid objects never squash.
- [ ] Artefact sweep done on every generated clip.

### Sources
- NIST, standard acceleration of gravity, 9.80665 m/s² (physics.nist.gov).
- Thomas & Johnston, *The Illusion of Life*; Richard Williams, *The Animator's Survival Kit* (gait and timing).
- Eye-blink rate studies (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18565090).
- "Do generative video models understand physical principles?" (arxiv.org/abs/2501.09038); VideoPhy (arxiv.org/abs/2406.03520); VBench (arxiv.org/abs/2311.17982).
- OpenAI, "Video generation models as world simulators" (known failures such as shattering glass).
- MIT Media Lab, Detect Fakes (artefact checklist).

<a id="sound-and-mix"></a>

## Sound and mix

`sound-and-mix`: Loudness targets, ducking, dialogue-to-music balance, where sound effects land, beat arithmetic and clean endings. Use when adding music, sound effects or voice to a video, and when reading the render's audio checks. (Which music suits the video is the user's choice.)

**Use when:** adding or placing music, sound effects or voice, and when the
render reports audio issues. Which music fits is decided with the user;
this skill is about levels, placement and timing.

### Rules
1. Integrated loudness by destination (ITU-R BS.1770 measurement): web and
   social about -14 LUFS with true peak at or under -1 dBTP; European
   broadcast -23 LUFS, -1 dBTP (EBU R 128); US broadcast -24 LKFS (ATSC A/85).
   Deliver one target per file; variants of the same video for the same
   destination match each other.
2. Speech must stay clearly above the music: keep the voice at least 7 dB
   above the bed, preferably 12 dB or more. Listeners, including hard-of-
   hearing listeners, rate the larger gap better.
3. Duck the music under speech: 12-20 dB lower; short attack (at most
   about 150 ms) and a release of a few hundred milliseconds; hold the duck
   through pauses shorter than about a second instead of pumping.
4. No sung lyrics under narration.
5. A sound effect belongs to a visible action and lands on it within ±1
   frame; audio never arrives more than about 45 ms before the picture
   (ITU-R BT.1359). A hit lands on the contact frame; a whoosh peaks at the
   fastest frame of the move.
6. Each sound effect must be audible over the bed in its first half second.
   One that sits under the music is noise, not design: raise it, lower the
   music, or remove it.
7. Beat arithmetic: frames per beat = fps × 60 ÷ BPM (120 BPM at 30 fps is
   15 frames). Compute each beat frame from its index and round once; put
   cuts on beats (or one frame before, `av-sync` rule 6) and scene changes
   on phrase boundaries (4 or 8 bars; a bar is four beats in most popular
   music).
8. Music ends on the end of a phrase, or fades over at least a second. Never
   stop it dead at the last frame.
9. Before a payoff, a short near-silence (0.3-0.75 s) makes it land.
10. Do not put a sound effect on every transition.
11. Never clip: if the render reports a peak-limited mix, lower the loudest
    sounds (usually sound effects) rather than pushing the limiter.

### In RenderWeld
- `audio.loudness` picks the preset: `social` (-14 LUFS; it limits peaks to
  -2 dBTP so the file still meets rule 1's -1 dBTP after AAC encoding), `broadcast-ebu`, `broadcast-atsc`, `podcast` or `off`.
  The finished file is measured; misses are in `audio.qa.issues`
  (`render.audio.loudnessQa` decides warn or fail).
- Ducking: `audio.music.ducking: true` or `{ depthDb, attackMs, releaseMs,
  thresholdDb }` (defaults 18 dB, 120 ms, 400 ms, -40 dB). It needs a voice.
- Balance: each track's `volume`, then bus gains `audio.gainDb.{voice,music,sfx}`.
  Fades: `audio.music.fadeInSeconds` and `fadeOutSeconds`.
- Sound effects: `audio.sfx: [{ asset, atFrame, volume }]`; `atFrame` is the
  contact frame of the picture event.
- Turn buses off for one render without editing the project:
  `render_project { audio: { music: false } }`, or `mute: true`.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- A whoosh on every cut; risers that lead nowhere.
- Music louder than the voice; a hard stop at the end.
- Sound effects you can see but not hear; clipped peaks.

### Before you render
- [ ] Loudness preset matches the destination; variants share it.
- [ ] Ducking on wherever music plays under speech.
- [ ] Every sound effect on its frame and audible; music ends on a phrase or fades.

### Sources
- EBU R 128 (tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r128-2014.pdf); ITU-R BS.1770; ATSC A/85.
- Spotify loudness normalisation (artists.spotify.com/help/article/loudness-normalization).
- ITU-R BT.1359 (detectability of audio ahead of video).
- Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research, 2026, on dialogue-to-background ratios (pubs.asha.org/doi/10.1044/2026_JSLHR-25-00127).
- Audacity Auto Duck defaults (manual.audacityteam.org/man/auto_duck.html).

<a id="voice-over"></a>

## Voice-over

`voice-over`: Pace, spoken-form text, pronunciation, pauses, emphasis and consent for narration, human or synthetic. Use when writing narration or generating text-to-speech.

**Use when:** writing narration or generating it with a text-to-speech provider.

### Rules
1. Pace about 150 words a minute (140-160); slower (130-150) for explainers;
   never above about 180.
2. Write text as it should be spoken: numbers, dates, units, currencies and
   abbreviations spelled out the way the narrator says them.
3. Keep a pronunciation list for the project: brand and product names,
   people, places and acronyms, with an alias or a phonetic spelling. Listen
   to every name in the generated audio.
4. Pauses: about a quarter second at a comma, 0.4-0.7 s at the end of a
   sentence, 0.8-1.5 s between sections. Use punctuation for pauses; avoid
   long runs of break tags, which make synthetic voices unstable.
5. One emphasised word per sentence, chosen on purpose.
6. Match the voice to the audience and the brand: accent for the audience's
   locale; the tone adjectives of the brief turned into settings and a
   reference read.
7. Generate two or three takes of important lines and keep the best.
8. Keep the word timings of the narration; they drive caption timing and the
   moment each visual appears (see `av-sync`).
9. Takes recorded or generated separately are joined on breaths with very
   short crossfades (5-20 ms) so there are no clicks.
10. A cloned or synthetic voice of a real person needs that person's written
    consent, confirmed by the user.
11. Do not narrate what the picture already says; narration adds what the
    picture cannot.

### In RenderWeld
- `generate_voice` (needs a configured text-to-speech provider and the
  user's agreement to its cost, `acknowledgeCost: true`) stores the audio as
  an asset with word timestamps; `set_audio { voice: { asset, startFrame } }`
  places it.
- Captions can come straight from those word timings (`get_captions`), so
  narration and captions stay in sync.
- One voice track per video: generate the whole narration in one call, or
  join separate takes in an audio editor first (rule 9) and upload the
  result with `upload_asset`.
- A voice longer than the video is cut at the end: fit the script first.
- Ducking (`audio.music.ducking`) keeps the music under the voice.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Identical intonation and sentence length throughout; a rising list cadence.
- Mispronounced brand names; no breaths, or breaths spliced mid-word.
- Talking wall to wall with no air.

### Before you render
- [ ] Pace measured in words a minute; pronunciation list applied and every name checked by ear.
- [ ] Voice fits the time available; no clicks at joins.
- [ ] Consent confirmed for any real person's voice.

### Sources
- ElevenLabs best practices: normalisation, pronunciation, pauses (elevenlabs.io/docs).
- W3C Pronunciation Lexicon Specification (w3.org/TR/pronunciation-lexicon) and SSML 1.1.
- BBC Subtitle Guidelines (speech rates).

<a id="captions-and-accessibility"></a>

## Captions and accessibility

`captions-and-accessibility`: Caption length, reading speed, timing, placement, line breaks, sound descriptions, audio description and flashing limits. Use for any video with speech, and any video with flashing or high-contrast patterns.

**Use when:** a video has speech, or contains flashes, strobes or striped
patterns.

### Rules
1. Every video with speech has captions (WCAG 2.2, 1.2.2). Give a sidecar
   file (WebVTT or SRT) where the platform takes one; burn them in as well for
   social video that autoplays without sound. Long-form video is never
   burned-in only.
2. Line length at most 42 characters, 32 on tall (portrait) frames; at most
   two lines.
3. Reading speed at most 20 characters a second for adults, 17 for children.
4. Each caption stays at least 5/6 s (0.83 s: 25 frames at 30 fps) and at
   most 7 s, longer than 5/6 s when rule 3 needs it, with a gap of at least
   two frames between captions; snap starts and ends to nearby cuts.
5. Sync: a caption appears with its speech, not before it by more than a
   moment, and never trails it by more than about 1.5 s.
6. Break lines at natural points: after punctuation, before conjunctions and
   prepositions; never split an article from its noun or a first name from a
   last name; the lower line may be longer.
7. Placement: bottom centre by default; move up for on-screen text, lower
   thirds and faces; on tall frames keep clear of the app's interface.
8. Style: a box or a strong outline behind the text, at least 4.5:1
   contrast. Identify speakers with labels or consistent colours.
9. Hard-of-hearing captions (SDH): speaker names and sounds in lowercase
   brackets ("[door slams]"), music described by mood; describe what is
   heard, not what is seen.
10. When the picture carries information that the audio does not, give an
    audio description (WCAG 1.2.5), or write the narration so it describes
    what matters.
11. Flashing: no more than three flashes in any one second, unless the
    flashing area is small (under about 25 % of a 10° field of view). Red
    flashes count separately and are worse. Avoid high-contrast stripes over
    large areas and long flashing sequences altogether (WCAG 2.2, 2.3.1).
12. Test anything that flashes with a photosensitivity analyser before
    publishing.

### In RenderWeld
- `captions.mode`: `off`, `burned`, `sidecar` or `both`; override for one
  render with `render_project { captions }`. Sidecars are SRT, WebVTT and ASS.
- Cues come from voice word timings (`generate_voice`), local speech-to-text
  (`transcribe_captions`), `import_captions` (SRT or WebVTT) or your own text.
- Caption QA follows the rules above (42 characters, 32 on portrait, two
  lines, 20 characters a second, 5/6 s to 7 s, two-frame gaps) and is
  reported by `get_captions` and in the render; fix every issue.
- Show the user the cue texts and times, ask for approval, then
  `update_captions { approve: true }`; never assume approval.
- Several languages: `update_captions { language, cues }`; `burnLanguage`
  picks the one burned in. Audio description: cues with `kind: "description"`
  (a WebVTT sidecar, never burned).
- Caption style (font, size, colours, box, outline) comes from the theme.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Bouncing word-by-word captions with emoji; captions over faces or the product.
- Blocks of uppercase text; no sound labels.
- Strobing "energy" transitions.

### Before you render
- [ ] Caption QA clean; names spelled correctly; the user approved the cues.
- [ ] Placement checked on every size; nothing under the platform interface.
- [ ] Audio description decided; no flashing over the limits.

### Sources
- Netflix Timed Text Style Guide and timing guidelines (partnerhelp.netflixstudios.com; backlothelp.netflix.com).
- BBC Subtitle Guidelines (bbc.co.uk/accessibility/forproducts/guides/subtitles).
- DCMP Captioning Key (dcmp.org/learn/captioningkey).
- US FCC caption quality standards, 47 CFR 79.1.
- W3C WCAG 2.2: 1.2.2, 1.2.5, 1.4.3, 2.3.1 (w3.org/TR/WCAG22).
- ITU-R BT.1702 (photosensitive epilepsy).

<a id="av-sync"></a>

## Audio and video sync

`av-sync`: Tolerances for sound against picture, frame arithmetic, aligning visuals to narration and beats, and checking the result. Use when timing visuals to voice, music or sound effects, and when checking a render.

**Use when:** timing a visual to a word, a beat or a sound, and when checking
a render.

### Rules
1. Tolerances: sound ahead of the picture is noticed at about 45 ms and
   unacceptable at about 90 ms; sound behind is noticed at about 125 ms and
   unacceptable at about 185 ms (ITU-R BT.1359). Those are what viewers notice,
   not targets: aim for zero and deliver within one frame, never with the
   sound early.
2. Keep the timeline in frames, at a constant frame rate, with 48 kHz audio.
   Convert seconds to frames once, from absolute times.
3. A visual that a word names appears at the start of that word, or up to
   about 0.2 s before it, never noticeably after. People tolerate the
   picture leading the sound far better than the reverse.
4. A bullet point appears at the start of its phrase and stays through the
   sentence.
5. An impact sound lands on the contact frame (±1); a whoosh peaks at the
   fastest frame of the move.
6. Beat frames: round(index × fps × 60 ÷ BPM + offset), where offset is the
   frame of the first downbeat (from the track's cue sheet, or found by ear
   and checked against the render; RenderWeld does not detect beats). Cut on the
   beat frame or one frame before it.
7. Characters: mouth shapes lead their sound by one or two frames; closures
   on M, B and P land exactly.
8. After rendering, measure: voice onsets against caption cues and visual
   events, and report the offset in milliseconds.

### In RenderWeld
- Every render checks that audio starts at 0 and that audio and video last
  the same within one frame (`checks.avSync`); a mismatch fails the render.
- `generate_voice` stores word timestamps; use them to place scene starts,
  bullet points and caption cues instead of estimating.
- Voice placement: `audio.voice.startFrame`; sound effects:
  `audio.sfx[].atFrame`. Both are frames, so compute them with rule 2.
- `validate_project` errors when a voice or sound effect starts after the end.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Narration describing a feature while the previous picture is still up.
- Cuts half a beat late; sound effects trailing the hit.
- Mouths moving without closing on M, B and P.

### Before you render
- [ ] Word timestamps used for every narration-driven visual.
- [ ] Beat grid computed if cutting to music.
- [ ] `checks.avSync` passes; measured offsets within one frame.

### Sources
- ITU-R BT.1359-1, relative timing of sound and vision (itu.int).
- EBU R 37 (broadcast chain targets).
- van Wassenhove et al. (2007), temporal window of audiovisual speech integration (doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2006.01.001).

<a id="brand-consistency"></a>

## Brand consistency

`brand-consistency`: Logo rules, colour tokens, type, motion and sound kept identical across scenes, sizes and a series. Use for any branded video, template or series.

**Use when:** the video belongs to a brand, or is part of a series.

### Rules
1. Collect the brand kit before designing: logo files (light, dark and
   single-colour; vector where possible), clear space and minimum size,
   colours with approved text-on-background pairs, fonts licensed for video,
   motion style, sound logo, tone of voice and anything banned.
2. Never stretch, rotate, recolour or add effects to a logo, and never
   animate it unless the kit supplies an animated version or motion rules.
   A logo the kit lets move is a rigid object: it never squashes
   (`physical-plausibility`).
3. Respect the kit's clear space (often a letter height or half the logo's
   height) and minimum size.
4. The logo keeps the same corner and size in every scene and every size,
   inside the safe area. An end card with logo and call to action holds at
   least 2 s.
5. In ads, show the brand early (within about 5 s), but do not open with a
   logo sting before the subject.
6. Colours come only from the kit's tokens: neutral backgrounds, one accent,
   every text colour checked for contrast against its background.
7. One motion style (fast and subtle, or expressive) with a fixed set of
   durations and curves; the same transition family across a series.
8. One music family, one sound logo and one voice per language for a series.
9. Images keep one grade, one lighting logic and one illustration style.
10. Build reusable scenes from the kit's values; never hard-code a colour or
    font that should come from the brand. Version the kit.

### In RenderWeld
- A theme is the brand kit in the renderer: `create_theme` with
  `colors` (background, surface, text, mutedText, accent, accent2),
  `fontFamily`, `headingWeight`, `motionSpeed` and caption style; apply it
  with `set_theme`. Templates and html scenes read the same tokens
  (`--rf-bg`, `--rf-text`, `--rf-muted`, `--rf-accent`, `--rf-font`,
  `--rf-heading-weight`, `--rf-speed`).
- Fonts: upload the font files as assets and name the family in the theme;
  they render offline in every engine and in burned captions.
- Logos: upload as assets (vector SVG is stored sanitised) and place them in
  the same pane or corner in every scene.
- Every size is a `variant` of the same project, so the brand stays identical
  across sizes.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Purple-to-blue gradients, glass blobs, neon glows.
- A pulsing or spinning logo; colours that are not in the kit.
- Stock footage of people high-fiving.

### Before you render
- [ ] Logo clear space and size checked; same position in every scene.
- [ ] Only theme colours used; contrast checked.
- [ ] Motion and sound consistent with the rest of the series.

### Sources
- W3C WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3 contrast.
- IBM Carbon motion: productive and expressive motion (carbondesignsystem.com).
- Google ad creative guidance on early branding (support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14783551).

<a id="review-and-qa"></a>

## Review and QA

`review-and-qa`: The professional editor's pass before a video is called final: technical checks, frames to look at, creative checks, findings and variants. Use before any render is delivered, and after any change to a delivered video.

**Use when:** before you call a render final, and after every change.
The renderer checks the file; you check whether the video works.

### Rules
1. Each output matches its spec: size, aspect ratio and a constant frame
   rate; duration within one frame of the plan.
2. Loudness and true peak on target; sound in sync within a frame; no
   flashing over the limits (see `captions-and-accessibility`).
3. Captions pass their checks, names are spelled right, and the user
   approved the cues.
4. Automatic checks: the first frame is not empty; no stretch over about 3 s
   without change; no text smaller than 2.6 % of the short side; no line on
   screen too briefly to read; a video over 15 s is not silent unless that
   was asked for.
5. Look at frames, not only reports: each scene at its start and middle,
   the frames on both sides of every cut, and the last frame, at phone size
   (360 px wide).
6. Creative checks: the subject is clear from the first frame; one message
   and one call to action; with text and sound off, the pictures still tell
   the story; a stranger could describe each key frame in one sentence.
7. Run the artefact sweep from `physical-plausibility` on every generated
   clip.
8. Every claim traces to the brief's sources; every asset has its licence;
   disclosure is applied where needed.
9. Write findings ranked P0 (must fix), P1 (should fix), P2 (nice to have),
   each with the time, the problem, the exact change, and what to keep. No
   scores.
10. Variants: re-lay out each size instead of cropping; an A/B test changes
    one thing (the opening, the call to action or the thumbnail).
11. Name outputs so they sort and explain themselves, e.g.
    `project_v003_9x16_en_hookB.mp4`; keep the project version each render
    was made from.

### In RenderWeld
- `validate_project`: errors block the render; read every warning.
- `preview_scene`: a low-resolution render of one scene or the whole
  project (per variant) to look at before the final render.
- `get_render_output`: `checks` (metadata, decode, duration, avSync,
  loudness), `audio.qa.issues`, caption QA, the poster image, the storage
  location and a download link.
- `get_captions`: cue QA. `list_project_versions`: what changed; each render
  records the project version it was made from.
- The `review_reel` prompt walks through this checklist with the manifest
  and the validation report.
- Every size is a `variant`: `render_project { variants: [...] }` renders
  them in one call.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Never watched at phone size; auto-crops cutting off heads.
- Juddering from a frame-rate mismatch; loudness that differs between variants.

### Before you deliver
- [ ] Technical: spec, checks, loudness, sync, captions, flashing.
- [ ] Frames: start, middle, cuts, last frame, at phone size.
- [ ] Creative: subject from frame one, one message, one call to action.
- [ ] Findings written as P0/P1/P2 and all P0s fixed.

### Sources
- YouTube recommended upload encoding settings (support.google.com/youtube/answer/1722171).
- Netflix, BBC and WCAG references in `captions-and-accessibility`.
- EBU R 128 and ITU-R BT.1359 references in `sound-and-mix` and `av-sync`.
